passage: I'm Keerthana, the neighbour across the landing, and I watched Anand from our open door. Anand's Amma had called out two jobs: blocks into the box, and finish the drawing before the food came. Anand laid the jobs out like two toys, chose the drawing because the crayons were already out, and coloured half a sun. Then a ball rolled past. The crayon dropped, and the blocks sat in their heap while the ball bounced. When the smell of dal reached the room, Anand stared at the half sun and started carrying blocks over, one by one.

qa.q: Which job did Anand choose to do first?
qa.a: Anand chose the drawing, because the crayons were already out.

qa.q: What might Anand have been feeling when the ball rolled past?
qa.a: Excited and pulled away: the crayon dropped at once, which suggests the ball felt far more fun than the half sun. Only Anand knows for sure.

qa.q: What small step could Anand's Amma try to help the plan hold next time?
qa.a: Let Anand point to the job that goes first, and move the ball out of sight until that job is done, so something shinier does not undo the choice.

qa.q: How does Keerthana make sense of the dropped crayon?
qa.a: Keerthana sees it as ordinary for a young child: putting jobs in order is new, and a bouncing ball easily beats a half-coloured sun.

grounding: A small child picks which job to do first by what is nearest and fun, and the order changes when a shinier thing appears.

passage:
Monday: Uma lined her tidy-up jobs along the rug, teddies first because teddies were her favourite. Halfway, the phone played a song and she ran off to dance. The teddies stayed in a heap.

Wednesday: her father Mohit asked, “What first, Uma?” She pointed at the crayons, then spotted a ladybird on the window and forgot the crayons for a long while.

Saturday: Uma put the crayon box on the table and announced, “Drawing first.” The ladybird crawled by again. “Bye-bye, later,” she whispered, and kept colouring. Mohit clapped once, very quietly, so as not to break her attention.

qa.q: What did Uma announce on Saturday?
qa.a: On Saturday Uma announced, “Drawing first.”

qa.q: Why might Uma have whispered “Bye-bye, later” to the ladybird?
qa.a: She wanted to keep looking at the ladybird but also wanted to finish her drawing, so she was saying goodbye to the shiny thing for now. She seems proud and a little tempted at once. 🙂

qa.q: What could Mohit try next to help Uma keep choosing an order?
qa.a: Keep asking “What first?” before each job and praise the choosing itself, since putting things in order is still new for Uma.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel when he claps quietly on Saturday?
qa.a: Mohit is probably pleased and hopeful, and he wants Uma to keep her focus, which is why he claps softly instead of loudly.

grounding: A young child chooses what to do first by fun and drops the plan when something shinier appears, over several days.

passage: Tejas squatted on the mud floor of the courtyard beside his wooden bullock cart, three marbles and a cloth ball. "Cart first," he told his sister Nikita, "because the cows will need it." He pushed the cart under the charpai. Then he picked up one marble, held it to the sun and forgot the rest. A goat wandered in through the gate. Tejas dropped the marble and ran after the goat, laughing. When Aaji called them for dinner, the ball and two marbles still lay in the dust. Nikita shook her head and scooped them into the basket.

qa.q: What did Tejas decide to put away first?
qa.a: Tejas decided to put the wooden bullock cart away first, pushing it under the charpai.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when the goat wandered in?
qa.a: He felt excited and playful; the goat was more fun than the marbles, so he dropped his plan and ran after it, laughing.

qa.q: What small step could help Tejas finish tidying next time?
qa.a: Someone could stay beside him and name one toy at a time, so the next thing to put away is always in front of him.

qa.q: How does Nikita see her brother's tidying?
qa.a: She seems a little exasperated but used to it, shaking her head and simply finishing the job by scooping the toys into the basket.

grounding: Illustrates a young child picking what to tidy first by what feels important, then dropping the plan when something more exciting appears.

passage: Rain tapped on the window of the small flat in Valencia. Mateo had two drawings on the table: a red fire truck and a half-coloured dog. "Truck first," he announced to Elif, the neighbour's girl who was visiting. "Trucks are faster." He coloured three wheels black. Then Elif opened a tin of glitter glue. Mateo's eyes went wide. He left the truck, grabbed the dog drawing and squeezed silver glitter all over its tail. "Now the dog is magic!" His mum called out that dinner was ready in five minutes. The truck still had one white wheel.

qa.q: What did Mateo draw on the two sheets?
qa.a: Mateo had a red fire truck and a half-coloured dog.

qa.q: How can you tell that Mateo felt thrilled when the glitter glue appeared?
qa.a: His eyes went wide and he dropped the truck straight away to cover the dog's tail, delighted that it was now magic. ✨

qa.q: What could Mateo's mum do to help him finish the truck another day?
qa.a: She could put the glitter away until the truck's last wheel is coloured, then let the glitter be the fun next step.

qa.q: What is it like for Elif when Mateo switches drawings?
qa.a: Elif probably enjoys it, since her glitter glue made the game more exciting and Mateo now wants to share it.

grounding: Shows a small child ordering tasks by what seems fun or urgent, with the plan switching when something shinier turns up.

passage: At the playschool, tidy-up song had started. Hafsa stood by the block corner and pointed. "First the big blocks, then the small ones," she told Sarita. She carried two big blocks to the shelf, very serious. On the way back she saw the dress-up box open, with a shiny gold crown on top. Hafsa put the crown on her head and twirled. The small blocks stayed on the rug. The teacher knelt down and said, "Queen Hafsa, can the crown help carry blocks?" Hafsa giggled, and together they carried the small blocks, one crown-wearing trip at a time.

qa.q: What did Hafsa plan to tidy first?
qa.a: Hafsa planned to tidy the big blocks first, then the small ones.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling when she saw the gold crown?
qa.a: She felt delighted and pulled away by it; the shiny crown was more exciting than the tidy-up, so she twirled instead of finishing.

qa.q: Which choice worked well for the teacher, and why?
qa.a: The teacher joined Hafsa's game instead of scolding, turning the crown into part of the tidying so the small blocks got carried after all.

qa.q: How might Sarita see Hafsa's plan?
qa.a: Sarita might find it funny that Hafsa sounded so sure about big blocks first and then left the small ones for a crown.

grounding: Illustrates a young child choosing a tidying order and changing it the moment something shinier catches her eye.

passage:
Monday. Harsha had to pack his toys for Nani's house. He put the red car in first, because it was fastest. Then he saw his kite and ran to the window with it. The bag stayed empty.
Wednesday. His big sister Ankita drew three pictures on a card: car, blocks, teddy. "One, two, three," she said. Harsha packed the car. He packed the blocks. Then the cat came in, and he chased the cat.
Saturday. Harsha held the card and packed car, blocks, teddy. He clapped. Then he unpacked the teddy to hug it.

qa.q: What did Ankita draw on the card?
qa.a: Car, blocks, teddy.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel when he finished packing on Saturday?
qa.a: Harsha felt happy and proud, clapping after packing all three.

qa.q: What helped Harsha keep an order, even for a little while?
qa.a: Ankita's picture card showed one, two, three, so Harsha had a simple order to follow when something shinier appeared.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel watching Harsha chase the cat on Wednesday?
qa.a: Ankita might feel amused and a little impatient, since the plan changed as soon as the cat came in.

grounding: Shows a young child choosing what to pack first by what is fun, and changing the plan whenever something shinier appears.
